headline: A single-author preprint solves the supersingular one-endomorphism problem in p^(1/3) time and memory with no heuristic, turning the cost isogeny-based cryptography already assumed into one it can prove.

items.title: Silicon pillars wick liquid nitrogen and hold a cryo chip 2.7 K above its bath
items.dek: Felix Mende and four co-authors modelled a silicon wick of 10-micrometre pillars flooded with liquid nitrogen under a cryogenic processor, and predict the chip sits 2.7 kelvin above the 77-kelvin boiling point at 20 watts per square centimetre.
items.why_it_matters: Cooling is the hidden tax on running logic cold, and the number that decides whether the tax is worth paying is the temperature difference between junction and coolant, not the coolant temperature itself. Pressing a cold plate onto the die through indium puts about 12 kelvin of that difference into solid-solid interfaces; removing the interfaces removes most of it. What takes over as the binding limit is geometric rather than thermal: the fluid can travel only a few millimetres before capillary pressure fails, so a cooled region has to be fed from its edges on that spacing, which turns a packaging decision into a floorplanning one.
items.background_md: Silicon transistors work better cold. Carrier mobility rises, subthreshold leakage falls, and the subthreshold swing — the gate voltage needed to change current tenfold — scales roughly with absolute temperature, so a circuit can run faster at the same power or at lower power for the same speed. Liquid nitrogen at 77 kelvin is the cheap way to get there. The obstacle is that the chip still dumps its own dissipation into that bath, and every kelvin of self-heating hands back part of what the cold was supposed to buy, so the figure that decides the argument is the junction-to-coolant difference.
items.deeper_md:
The wick is an array of cylindrical silicon pillars — 10 µm diameter, 24 µm pitch, 75 µm tall — standing in saturated liquid nitrogen at 77.36 K. Capillary pressure pulls fluid up between them, and evaporation happens in the thin film that wets each pillar near the three-phase contact line, which is where essentially all the thermal resistance sits: silicon near 77 K conducts at over 1400 W/m·K, so the solid is not the bottleneck. The model chains a Young–Laplace meniscus shape into a Hertz–Knudsen–Schrage interfacial flux with an accommodation coefficient near 0.74, then into a unit cell and an array-level thermo-hydraulic solve.

At 20 W/cm² that gives 2.7 K of superheat and an areal resistance around 0.135 K·cm²/W, against roughly 12 K for a pressed-indium conduction path and 8.3 K for pool boiling on a flat surface. Pillar height barely matters; pitch-to-diameter ratio and contact angle dominate. Single-fed dry-out length is about 2.7 mm, or a 5.3 mm double-fed width — water in the same geometry reaches 18.1 mm.

Nothing here was measured. The accommodation coefficient is a theoretical estimate, the vapour model is flagged as unreliable above roughly 6 K of superheat, and Marangoni stresses are omitted at Marangoni numbers of 322–409, a range where comparable water studies moved wall temperature by some 14 percent. The authors put cryogenic wetting measurements first on their own list.

glossary.definition: The point where the suction a meniscus can generate stops delivering liquid as fast as evaporation removes it, so the far end of the wick empties and the surface above it overheats.

Evaporation from the micrometre-thick liquid wedge where solid, liquid and vapour meet; the conduction path through the liquid is shortest there, so most of the heat leaves through a small fraction of the area.
Power dissipated per unit chip area. It, rather than total watts, decides how hard a cooling scheme is, because the removal path has a fixed footprint to work through.

A kinetic expression for how fast molecules cross a liquid–vapour interface, scaled by an accommodation coefficient giving the fraction of arriving molecules that actually condense rather than bouncing.

items.fab_angle: A 75 µm pillar at 10 µm diameter is a 7.5:1 deep-RIE job on bare silicon, well inside what a teaching cleanroom's Bosch process reaches. The parameters that decide whether it works are not etch depth but sidewall scallop and the contact angle of the surface afterwards, so the interesting measurement is a wetting test after the release, not a cross-section.

items.title: Grow the p-type oxide faster, not hotter, and the Ga₂O₃ diode conducts better
items.dek: Dagny Sacksteder and six co-authors grew the nickel-oxide p-type layer of a gallium-oxide power diode by molecular beam epitaxy rather than by sputtering, and report that raising the growth rate to 380 nanometres an hour, not raising the temperature, is what lowers on-resistance.
items.why_it_matters: The p-side of every gallium-oxide junction arrives as a deposited film, so junction quality is decided by a deposition recipe instead of by an implant and an anneal — and the usual recipe, reactive sputtering, bombards the very surface it is trying to form a junction with. Epitaxy takes the bombardment away. The finding that the effective lever is deposition rate rather than substrate temperature matters because temperature is the shared lever: it is spent against everything already built on the wafer. A knob that buys interface quality without drawing on thermal budget is one that remains usable late in a flow.
items.background_md: A power diode has to block kilovolts when off and conduct with little loss when on, and the two demands fight each other: blocking wants a thick, lightly doped drift region, and that same region is what current must cross. Widening the bandgap raises the electric field the material survives before avalanche, so the drift layer can be thinner and more heavily doped at the same voltage rating. That is the case for gallium oxide, whose bandgap near 4.9 electronvolts puts its theoretical figure of merit above silicon carbide and gallium nitride — and whose crystal refuses acceptors, so holes must be supplied by a second material laid on top.
items.deeper_md:
At 380 nm/hr the 35 nm p⁻ NiO layers give a device-average specific on-state resistance of 1.46 Ω·cm² and an ideality factor of 1.46, with the best individual device at 25 mΩ·cm² and a rectification ratio of 2.7×10⁶. Growth rates went to 600 nm/hr without degrading film quality, while raising substrate temperature produced no measurable improvement. Cross-sectional STEM shows the (100) NiO on (100) β-Ga₂O₃ interface coherent and atomically abrupt, which is the actual claim — an interface, not a device.

Hold the numbers against the field. Gilankar and co-workers report a NiO/Ga₂O₃ diode blocking above 3 kV at 4.4 mΩ·cm², a unipolar figure of merit past 2 GW/cm², and sub-1 V turn-on; that is roughly 330× lower specific resistance than this paper's device average. No breakdown voltage is reported here at all, and the authors call their diodes unoptimized in the abstract.

The 58× spread between the average die and the best die is the result that most needs explaining, since a growth process is only useful if it is uniform, and the preprint does not account for it. The same NREL-led group previously showed that a spinel NiGa₂O₄ layer forms at this interface at 550 °C, so what the interface looks like after a device has been run hot is a separate question from what it looks like as grown.

glossary.definition: A power device's on-state resistance multiplied by its active area, in Ω·cm². Normalising by area is what lets two devices of different size be compared at all.
How far a diode's forward current departs from the ideal exponential law; n near 1 means diffusion-limited current, and values well above 1 point at recombination or a defective, resistive interface.

Nickel oxide conducts by holes because nickel vacancies leave states near its valence band, which makes it the standard way to put a p-layer onto an oxide semiconductor that will not accept acceptors itself.
Breakdown voltage squared divided by specific on-resistance, in W/cm². It compresses the blocking-versus-conduction trade into one number, which is how materials get ranked against each other.

items.fab_angle: Plasma damage from a sputtered film is invisible to a thickness measurement and shows up only in the device. Ideality factor and reverse leakage on a plain diode are the cheapest probe a teaching lab has for whether a deposition step is wrecking the surface underneath it, and both come off a probe station with no special tooling.

items.title: Approximating the netlist as well as the algorithm buys 11% at a fixed error
items.dek: Jian Shi and four co-authors built HALS, a tool that lets a chip compiler approximate a circuit at the gate level as well as at the algorithm level, and report 11.3 percent lower hardware cost than the best prior approximate synthesis methods at the same error bound.
items.why_it_matters: Approximate design has been two trades that do not speak to each other: a behavioural compiler can delete an operation from a dataflow graph, a netlist optimiser can delete a gate, and each prices its own moves against an accuracy budget it controls alone. Run them one after the other and the first commits the design to a structure before the second is allowed to say what that structure costs. Making gate-level moves visible inside the behavioural search turns the accuracy budget into a single shared currency, which is why the same permitted inaccuracy yields smaller silicon instead of one stage quietly undoing the other's choice.
items.background_md: Plenty of computations do not need exact answers. An image filter, a neural-network layer or a sensor front end already consumes noisy data and feeds something tolerant, so a circuit that is wrong in the last bit some fraction of the time can be perfectly acceptable — and it can be considerably smaller, because the carry chains and comparison logic that guarantee that last bit are where much of an arithmetic unit's area and critical path live. Approximate synthesis is the practice of selling that guarantee for area, power or timing under a stated numerical error bound, so the trade is auditable rather than accidental.
items.deeper_md:
HALS partitions a control-and-dataflow graph into sub-graphs, builds local and global error models, runs approximate logic synthesis inside each sub-graph, and then picks candidates with a greedy design-space exploration ranked on cost-to-error ratio. Against ADVISOR and PreDAC on fourteen benchmarks drawn from S2CBench, PaderBench and PolyBench, under matched error constraints expressed in MAE, MSE, MAPE, SNR and PSNR, it reports an 11.32 percent average hardware-cost reduction under tight bounds and 6.34 percent under loose ones.

Both spoilers are named by the authors. The gains collapse wherever the partitioner struggles: the FFT's butterfly network is too densely connected, so secondary partitioning duplicates logic, and the pipelined decimation design resists for the same reason. And runtime is dominated by the gate-level step, which scales with the gate count of a sub-graph rather than with total circuit area — conv3x3 could not be partitioned at all and took 20,112 seconds, against roughly 18.5 seconds for fir9. A three-order-of-magnitude runtime spread inside one benchmark suite is the practical limit on where this can be pointed, and the proposed fix, a duplication factor that decides when to skip partitioning, is future work rather than a result.

glossary.definition: A compiler that turns C-like behavioural code into a register-transfer-level circuit, choosing the schedule and which hardware gets shared; the approximate variant additionally weakens or deletes operations.
Gate-level optimisation that removes or rewires gates in a finished netlist and accepts a bounded output error in exchange for area, delay or power.
The intermediate form a behavioural compiler works on, with nodes for operations and edges for data and control dependence. It is the level at which an operation can be dropped wholesale.
Two of the accuracy yardsticks used here — mean absolute percentage error, and peak signal-to-noise ratio in decibels, which is how image blocks state how wrong they are permitted to be.

items.fab_angle: The same measurement is available on an open PDK without any of this machinery: synthesise an adder twice, once exact and once with the low-order bits tied off, and read the area and slack difference straight out of the report. The trade HALS automates is visible in two runs of a free tool, which is also how you find out whether your design was ever accuracy-limited.

items.title: MoE decoding is weight movement, so the weights get quantised into a codebook
items.dek: Bin Ma, Wenjie Fan and Dong Li measured that loading expert weights takes 56 percent of the time to generate a token from Qwen3-30B-A3B on an AWS Trainium3 chip, and shrank those weights about four-fold with a codebook so the chip's engines stop waiting.
items.why_it_matters: A mixture-of-experts model is built to avoid arithmetic: only a few of its expert blocks run for any given token, so multiplies per token stay small while parameter count does not. That bargain holds while a batch is big enough to reuse an expert's parameters across many tokens, and it inverts at batch one, where each expert touched is pulled out of high-bandwidth memory and used once. The remedy here is not faster memory but fewer bytes — four bits of index per parameter instead of sixteen, with the arithmetic still done in wide precision after lookup. The resource being bought back is bandwidth, not FLOPs.
items.background_md: An accelerator with a software-managed scratchpad has no cache to cover a mistake: the compiler states exactly which bytes move from high-bandwidth memory into on-chip SRAM and when, so any parameter fetched and used once pays its full trip. Generating text one token at a time is the worst case for that, because each step performs only a handful of multiplies against every parameter it touches. Arithmetic intensity — useful operations per byte fetched — is what decides whether a matrix engine is fed or idle, and at batch one it sits near the floor.
items.deeper_md:
The representation is a vector-quantised term plus a low-rank term shared across a layer's experts: blocks of d ∈ {4, 8} weights become one uint8 index into a 256-entry codebook, and the residual rides on a rank-r basis common to the layer. Bits per original weight come out as b(d,r) = 8/d + 16r/H + 16r/(EI) + 16Kd/(EHI), landing near 4 bits for a 3.92–4.92× storage reduction across five model families.

The target is an AWS Trainium3 NeuronCore-v4 with 32 MiB of SBUF, 4.7 TB/s of HBM bandwidth and sixteen DMA engines, and the point of the multi-engine dataflow is that dequantisation runs on the vector and scalar engines while the tensor engine is busy, so decompression does not become a new serial stage. Batch-one speedups are 1.15–1.31× over AWS's dense BF16 MoE megakernels and 1.09–2.07× over PyTorch/XLA, reaching 1.70× at batch 16, and WikiText-103 perplexity comes in 2.7 to 4.9 percent below the BF16 teacher after distillation.

Three limits the authors state: prefill is untouched because it is compute-bound, down-projection weights stay in BF16, and the schedule is chosen by offline profiling per model, so the result is a tuned artefact rather than a general compiler pass.

glossary.definition: A layer holding many parallel weight blocks of which a router picks a few per token, so parameter count can grow without the multiply count growing with it.
Explicitly addressed on-chip SRAM with no automatic caching. Every transfer into it is scheduled by the compiler, so a wasted fetch is never quietly absorbed by hardware.
Useful arithmetic operations per byte moved from memory. Below the machine's own ratio of peak operations to peak bandwidth, a kernel is bandwidth-bound however fast the arithmetic is.
Replacing a block of weights with the index of the nearest entry in a shared codebook, so storage costs log₂(codebook size) bits per block rather than per individual weight.

items.title: A supersingular curve gives up an endomorphism in p^(1/3), with no heuristic
items.dek: José Luis Delgado gives an algorithm that finds a non-scalar endomorphism of a supersingular elliptic curve — the hard problem underneath isogeny-based post-quantum cryptography — in about p^(1/3) time and memory, proved without any smoothness assumption.
items.why_it_matters: Parameter sizes are chosen against the best attack anybody can prove, not the best one anybody believes in, so the distance between a heuristic exponent of 1/3 and a proved exponent of 2/5 was a real distance: designers either leaned on the heuristic or paid for the weaker theorem. Removing it removes that choice. The storage bound is the more interesting half — this method stores as much as it computes, and an attack requiring that much storage is much harder to mount than one merely requiring that many operations, which is a distinction key-size arguments now have to make out loud.
items.background_md: Most deployed public-key cryptography rests on problems a large quantum computer would dissolve, so the field has been replacing it. One replacement family uses isogenies — maps between elliptic curves that preserve the group law. Supersingular curves over a field of size p² form a graph whose vertices are curves and whose edges are small-degree isogenies, and that graph behaves like an expander, meaning a short random walk lands essentially anywhere, so finding a path between two named curves looks hard. Equivalent to that path problem is computing a curve's endomorphism ring, the set of maps from the curve to itself, and that is what attacks actually go after.
items.deeper_md:
The target is the OneEnd problem: produce a single non-scalar endomorphism of a supersingular curve E over 𝔽_{p²}. Page and Wesolowski proved OneEnd and the full endomorphism-ring problem equivalent under probabilistic polynomial-time reductions, so one endomorphism is the whole ring.

The generic classical cost sat at p^(1/2+o(1)) for years. Wesolowski reached exponent 1/3 under a heuristic about smooth integers; Udovenko reached 2/5 unconditionally. This preprint reaches p^(1/3)·exp(O(√(log p · log log p))) in both time and memory with neither assumption.

The mechanism is to stop hoping for smoothness. Rather than assume a minimal-degree isogeny happens to factor into small primes, the algorithm fixes a family of squarefree degrees in advance that are products of small primes, enumerates isogenies of those degrees out of E and out of its Frobenius conjugate E^(p), and matches the two lists by colour-coding; composing a match with Frobenius yields an endomorphism. What makes it unconditional is a counting theorem bounding how often two such isogenies land on the same curve, proved by embedding the composite into a quadratic order.

Caveats: this is an unrefereed ePrint-style preprint, and the exponent only matches what the field already assumed, so nothing deployed is weaker today than it was last week.

glossary.definition: A map between two elliptic curves that sends identity to identity and respects addition; its degree counts how many points collapse together, and low-degree isogenies are the edges attacks walk along.

All the isogenies from a curve to itself, under addition and composition. For supersingular curves it is large and non-commutative, and knowing it breaks the hardness assumption these schemes rest on.
A cost growing as the cube root of the field characteristic, up to a factor smaller than any power of p. The exponent, not the sub-exponential factor, is what key sizes get chosen against.
The unproved assumption that a number arising mid-computation factors entirely into small primes about as often as a random number of its size would — convenient, standard, and not a theorem.

items.title: Google routes inference on predicted latency, not load, and runs 20% hotter
items.dek: Santiago Balseiro, Bartek Wydrowski and twelve colleagues at Google describe DLB, the load balancer that has routed its generative-AI inference for 22 months by learning a requests-in-flight-to-latency curve per server, and report 17 percent lower median latency than the system it replaced.
items.why_it_matters: Routing on processor utilisation works when every request costs roughly the same. Generative serving breaks that twice: prompt processing and token generation have different cost shapes, and two calls to one model can differ by orders of magnitude in how many tokens come out. What DLB steers on instead is a fitted map from a replica's in-flight count to the delay a new arrival would see — flat while the replica is idle, linear once it saturates — so the router prices its own decision rather than reading a stale gauge. The measurable consequence is headroom: the same fleet is held roughly 20 percent closer to saturation.
items.background_md: A load balancer decides which of many replicas serves each request, and the classic answers — send it to the least-loaded server, or to the less loaded of two probed at random — assume load stands in for how long a request will wait. That assumption holds when service times are short and similar to each other. When they are not, the queue a request joins matters more than the utilisation of the machine behind it, and a router reading a utilisation figure sampled tens of seconds earlier is steering by a quantity that has already moved.
items.deeper_md:
DLB replaces MNLB, Google's global balancer, which recomputed routing weights to minimise network latency subject to serving-capacity constraints on a cadence of tens of seconds. DLB probes instead: root routers poll leaf routers every few milliseconds, leaves return requests-in-flight, error rates and a fitted latency model, and router replicas share probe results peer-to-peer so one probe informs many decisions — the trick Prequal used to make power-of-d-choices affordable at scale.

The model is a softplus fit of latency against requests-in-flight, which captures latency that is near-constant at low occupancy and linear once queuing starts. Three cost functions are offered: in-flight count per replica, expected latency plus network round trip, and inverse marginal service rate plus round trip. The gradient form wins overall in simulation, while the plain in-flight form stays competitive at high utilisation and is worse at low.

Across 68 production endpoints the migration gives 17 percent lower p50, 13 percent lower mean, 14 percent at p90 and 13 percent at p95. The authors name the flaw themselves: the latency model is fitted only on requests the router chose to send, so it is censored toward short queries, and correcting that is an exploration problem they leave open.

glossary.definition: How many requests a replica is working on right now. Unlike processor utilisation it is observable by the router itself and updates the instant the router makes a decision.
Probe d replicas at random and send the request to the best of them; it recovers most of the benefit of probing every replica for a small fraction of the probing cost.
The median and 95th-percentile latency across a population of requests. Service objectives are written against the tail, because the median hides exactly the requests users notice.
The smooth function log(1 + eˣ), used here because it is flat on one side and linear on the other, which is the shape latency takes as a server fills up.

foundations.subtitle: Making pitches the exposure tool cannot resolve, by letting a deposited film be the real mask.
foundations.tldr: A 193 nm immersion scanner cannot resolve finer than about 38 nm half-pitch, and the industry has been building circuits at a third of that for a decade. Multipatterning is how: print a coarse pattern the tool can actually resolve, then use deposition and etch to turn every printed line into two, or four. The consequence is that the half-pitch stops being set by the exposure and starts being set by the thickness of a film — which is both the trick and the new set of problems.

sections.heading: The pitch the tool can print
sections.body_md:
Start from Rayleigh, because everything else is a response to it. The smallest half-pitch a projection printer can resolve is k₁·λ/NA: the wavelength divided by the numerical aperture, scaled by a process factor k₁ that captures illumination, resist and mask engineering. At 193 nm with water immersion, NA stops at about 1.35, because the fluid's refractive index caps it. ASML's TWINSCAN NXT:2050i, a 1.35 NA immersion scanner, quotes production resolution of 40 nm with quadrupole illumination and 38 nm with dipole.

That 38 nm is a half-pitch, so the finest line-and-space the tool prints in one shot has a 76 nm period. And k₁ has a hard floor of 0.25, because below that the two interfering diffraction orders you need simply do not both make it through the pupil. There is no optical move left at 193 nm. Meanwhile fins and metal lines are wanted at 30 to 40 nm pitch. The gap is a factor of two to four, and it has to be closed by chemistry and etch rather than by optics.
sections.deeper_md: It is worth being precise about which number is quoted where, because half-pitch and pitch get swapped constantly. ASML's 38 nm dipole figure is half-pitch: 38 nm of line plus 38 nm of space, period 76 nm. When Mark LaPedus writes that "193nm immersion and double patterning" reaches a minimum pitch of 38 nm, that is a full pitch — one round of pitch division applied to the 76 nm the scanner can print. The two numbers are the same number seen from either side of the division, and confusing them makes a process look either twice as good or twice as bad as it is.

sections.heading: Print it twice, and pay in overlay
sections.body_md:
The obvious approach is litho-etch-litho-etch. Split the target layout into two masks, each carrying lines at twice the final pitch, which the scanner can resolve comfortably. Expose the first, etch it into a hard mask, coat again, expose the second interleaved between the first, etch again. Two exposures, two etches, one final pitch half what either exposure printed.

What you have bought is a new dimension that did not exist before: the placement of the second exposure relative to the first. The NXT:2050i quotes 2.5 nm cross-matching on-product overlay, and that entire budget lands directly on the spaces between an A line and a B line. A 1 nm placement error makes one space 1 nm wider and its neighbour 1 nm narrower. The lines are fine; the spaces alternate, and it is the spaces that set capacitance and breakdown.
sections.deeper_md: There is a second cost, and it lands on software. Assigning every polygon in a layout to one of two masks so that no two same-mask shapes sit closer than the single-exposure limit is graph colouring: build a graph with an edge between every too-close pair and two-colour it. Layouts containing an odd cycle have no legal assignment at all. The usual escape is a stitch — split one shape across both masks and rely on the two halves overlapping — which converts a colouring conflict into a place where overlay error becomes a line-width error. Yu and Pan's framework generalises this to K masks with semidefinite programming, and the reason design rules at these nodes are so restrictive is precisely that the layout has to be decomposable before it can be manufactured.

sections.heading: The spacer trick: the mask becomes a film thickness
sections.body_md:
Self-aligned double patterning takes a different route. Print a sacrificial line — a mandrel — at twice the target pitch, which the scanner handles easily. Deposit a conformal film over it, thin and uniform, usually by atomic layer deposition, which controls thickness to a few ångströms because it grows one self-limiting monolayer per cycle. Then etch that film anisotropically with no mask at all: the vertical ion flux clears it from horizontal surfaces while leaving it standing on every vertical sidewall. Strip the mandrel out from between them, and each printed line has become two.

Two things changed. The width of each final line is now the deposited film thickness, not an exposure result, so its uniformity is a deposition problem instead of a dose-and-focus problem. And the two lines derived from one mandrel are positioned by that mandrel's own edges, so there is no alignment step between them and no overlay error to spend. That is what "self-aligned" means.
sections.deeper_md: The geometry is worth doing by hand once. Let the mandrel have width M, the space between mandrels be G, and the spacer thickness be S, so the mandrel pitch is P = M + G. After the mandrel is removed, each period contains two spacer lines of width S and two spaces: one of width M, where the mandrel used to be, and one of width G − 2S, between neighbouring mandrels with a spacer eating into each side. Equal line and space requires S = M = G − 2S, which gives G = 3S and P = 4S — so the final pitch is 2S and the final half-pitch is exactly the deposited thickness. That identity is the whole idea, stated in one line.

sections.heading: Pitch walking: the error no alignment fixes
sections.body_md:
Look again at those two spaces. One is M, set by lithography and mandrel etch. The other is G − 2S, set by lithography, mandrel etch and film thickness. They are produced by different steps, so they are never exactly equal, and the result is a pattern whose spaces alternate wide-narrow-wide-narrow all the way across the wafer. This is pitch walking, and the important thing about it is that nothing is misaligned. No alignment step can remove it, because there is no alignment step involved.

Do the sensitivity. Hold the mandrel pitch fixed and let the mandrel print δ too wide, so G shrinks by δ. One space becomes M + δ, the other M − δ: a 1 nm mandrel CD error yields a 2 nm space asymmetry. Let the spacer come out ε too thick instead, and the line grows by ε while one space shrinks by 2ε. Every process error is doubled on its way to the thing that matters.
sections.deeper_md: Because the deviation is systematic rather than random, it is measurable — if you can measure it fast enough to feed back. TSMC's published method for mandrel and spacer patterning is essentially about that: rather than trying to map main-array measurements back to the steps that caused them, it adds short dedicated "pitch monitor" structures with distinctive loop shapes, sized to fit inside a single metrology field so a tool can read the pitch deviation quickly and attribute it. The patent lists the contributing knobs explicitly — photolithography conditions, mandrel width and spacing, spacer thickness, etch selectivity — which is a fair summary of why the effect is hard to null out: four independent steps, one output.

sections.heading: Doing it twice: SAQP
sections.body_md:
The output of one round is a set of lines, and lines can serve as mandrels. Do it again and the pitch divides again: 76 nm from the scanner becomes 38 nm, becomes 19 nm. That is self-aligned quadruple patterning, and it is how sub-10 nm-class fins and 3D NAND word lines get made without an EUV tool anywhere in the flow.

The dimensions are unremarkable individually. IBM's SAQP patent gives representative ranges: first mandrels 30 to 60 nm wide, first spacer 15 to 30 nm, second spacer 10 to 30 nm, final fins 5 to 50 nm. A spacer-on-spacer variant from TEL's Albany centre reported 15 nm lines on a 30 nm pitch while dropping a sacrificial layer, which they argue gives better control of pitch walking than conventional SAQP. The cost is the chain: one exposure, then roughly a dozen deposition and etch steps, each adding its own variation to a budget that is already doubled by the geometry.
sections.deeper_md: The reason this survived the arrival of EUV is arithmetic rather than sentiment. LaPedus reports single-patterning EUV starting around 38 or 36 nm pitch and running out somewhere between 32 and 30 nm, with EUV double patterning needed at the 26 nm pitch that 5 nm-node metal layers want. So EUV does not abolish pitch division; it starts the division from a finer number. And every round of EUV double patterning reintroduces exactly the overlay problem that the self-aligned approach was invented to avoid, on a tool whose exposures cost considerably more, which is why spacer schemes remain the cheaper answer wherever the pattern is a regular grating.

sections.heading: What a spacer cannot do: ends
sections.body_md:
There is one thing a spacer fundamentally cannot make, and it decides the shape of everything downstream. A conformal film deposited on a mandrel wraps all the way around it, so after the anisotropic etch and the mandrel strip you are left with closed loops, not lines. Every line end in the final circuit has to be created by a separate cut or block exposure that removes a piece of the loop.

So the hard problem has moved rather than vanished. Pitch is now set by a film thickness and needs no alignment; line ends are set by a second exposure and need all the alignment there is. The budget that binds is edge placement error — the total misregistration between a feature defined by one step and a feature defined by another — and it is why, as LaPedus puts it, EUV does not solve the edge placement error problem. It is also why the design side cannot be separated from the process side here: the layout must be decomposable, colourable and cuttable before it is manufacturable at all.
sections.deeper_md: Two habits of mind are worth carrying away. First, every one of these schemes trades a lithography problem for a deposition-and-etch problem, and the trade is usually good because film thickness is controllable to ångströms while exposure dose and focus are not. Second, the trade is never free: it converts a random error into a systematic one. Overlay in a double-exposure scheme is random from wafer to wafer and can be corrected by a feedback loop; pitch walking in a spacer scheme is baked into the geometry and repeats identically on every die, so it shows up as a fixed offset in device characteristics rather than as scatter. Which of those two a process engineer prefers depends entirely on whether the downstream device can be designed around a known bias.

glossary.definition: Pitch is the repeat distance of a line-and-space array; half-pitch is half of it, and equals the line width when lines and spaces are equal. Scanner resolution specifications are quoted as half-pitch, process nodes usually as pitch.

The dimensionless coefficient in half-pitch = k₁·λ/NA that absorbs illumination shape, resist contrast and mask enhancement. It has a hard physical floor of 0.25 for single exposure, because below that the diffraction orders needed to form an image no longer both fit in the pupil.

The sacrificial line printed by lithography that a spacer is deposited against. It is removed before the pattern is transferred, so its width survives only as one of the two space widths in the final array.

The conformal film left standing on a mandrel's sidewalls after an unmasked anisotropic etch clears it from horizontal surfaces. Its deposited thickness becomes the final line width, which is why the deposition tool inherits the CD uniformity job from the scanner.

Systematic alternation between two space widths in a spacer-defined array, because the space where the mandrel was and the space between mandrels are set by different process steps. It is not misalignment and cannot be corrected by alignment.

Pitch division by two separate exposures interleaved with each other, each at relaxed pitch. Simple to understand and expensive in both passes and overlay budget, since the placement of the second exposure directly sets the spaces.
An extra exposure whose only job is to delete material — breaking spacer loops into line ends, or removing unwanted fins. It is where overlay re-enters a self-aligned flow.

The total misregistration between the edge of a feature defined by one patterning step and the edge of a feature defined by another, combining overlay, CD variation and etch bias. At these pitches it is the budget that actually binds.

foundations.try_this: Do the SADP arithmetic against the club's own stepper, then go and measure the film that would be the mask. First the arithmetic: find the finest line-and-space your maskless tool actually resolves — a dose-and-focus matrix printed on the resist you have on the shelf, read out on the microscope — and call that half-pitch H. One round of SADP takes you to H/2 and two rounds to H/4, so write down what pitch your tool would reach at 19 nm-class ratios and see how far that is from the 30 nm pitch TEL reported with 15 nm lines. Then do the sensitivity by hand from the section above: with mandrel width M, gap G and spacer thickness S, show that equal line and space requires G = 3S and that the final half-pitch is exactly S, then perturb M by 1 nm and confirm the two spaces separate by 2 nm. Second, the measurement: the spacer is just a conformal film, so grow a thermal oxide in the tube furnace at a thickness you can predict from Deal–Grove, and read the thickness back from the interference colour — that number's run-to-run spread is exactly the CD uniformity a spacer process would inherit. Finally, open US9305845B2 on Google Patents, which is free, and follow the figures step by step; the drawings are the clearest free illustration of the mandrel-spacer-mandrel-spacer sequence anywhere.
